name: Second Bank of the United States
subject: us-history

lesson.title: Jackson vs. Biddle: The Bank War That Reshaped American Finance
lesson.summary: Jackson's veto of the Second Bank's recharter and his later withdrawal of federal deposits destroyed the national bank he saw as a tool of privileged elites, reshaping American banking for a generation.
lesson.body:
The Second Bank of the United States was a federally chartered institution created in 1816, during James Madison's presidency, to stabilize the young nation's currency, manage government funds, and provide credit for economic growth. It followed the model of Alexander Hamilton's First Bank of the United States, chartered in 1791, whose own twenty year charter had been allowed to lapse in 1811 amid disputes over its constitutionality, disputes that reflected the older debate between Hamilton and Jefferson over how much economic power the federal government should hold.

The bank's constitutionality was tested and upheld in the Supreme Court case McCulloch v. Maryland in 1819, in which Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that Congress had implied power under the Constitution to charter a national bank and that the state of Maryland could not tax a federal institution, since, in Marshall's words, the power to tax involves the power to destroy. Nicholas Biddle became the bank's president in 1823 and ran it with real skill, using it to regulate the money supply by controlling how freely state banks could issue currency, but he also became known for wielding the bank's financial influence in ways that made him politically powerful and, to critics, dangerously unaccountable.

Andrew Jackson viewed the bank with deep suspicion from early in his presidency, seeing it as an unconstitutional concentration of financial power that favored wealthy Northeastern investors and speculators over ordinary farmers and workers, a view consistent with the broader Jacksonian Democracy suspicion of privileged, unaccountable institutions. He also distrusted the way a private, profit seeking corporation controlled so much of the nation's financial system with minimal public oversight.

The conflict came to a head in what became known as the Bank War. Henry Clay and Daniel Webster, hoping to force Jackson into a politically damaging position ahead of the 1832 election, pushed a bill through Congress to recharter the bank four years early, betting that Jackson would not dare veto a popular institution. Jackson vetoed it anyway, issuing a forceful message that attacked the bank as a tool of privilege and cast the veto as a defense of ordinary Americans against entrenched elites. Rather than hurting him, the veto became a centerpiece of his reelection campaign, and Jackson won a decisive victory over Clay in 1832.

Jackson treated his reelection as a mandate against the bank and moved to cripple it well before its charter was due to expire, ordering the withdrawal of federal deposits starting in 1833 and redistributing them into a collection of state chartered banks that critics mockingly called pet banks. The bank's federal charter lapsed in 1836, and Biddle kept it running afterward only as an ordinary Pennsylvania chartered institution before it eventually failed. The resulting instability in currency and credit, worsened by other factors such as Jackson's Specie Circular requiring gold or silver for public land purchases, contributed to the Panic of 1837, a severe economic depression that struck shortly after Jackson left office and became one of the lasting, contested legacies of his war against the national bank.
